summary: This comprehensive review surveys crosstalk phenomena across six major quantum computing platforms—superconducting circuits, trapped ions, neutral atoms, photonics, semiconductors, and nitrogen vacancy centres—examining physical origins, characterization methods, and mitigation strategies. The authors document platform-specific crosstalk mechanisms (always-on $ZZ$ interactions in superconductors, pulse spillover in trapped ions, frequency crowding in semiconductors) and discuss security vulnerabilities enabling adversarial attacks and information leakage in multi-tenant quantum processors.
motivation: As quantum processors scale beyond a few qubits, crosstalk-induced correlated errors become a dominant noise source limiting performance, yet detailed treatment of crosstalk is often neglected in device characterization and algorithm execution across different platforms. A unified, platform-comparative treatment was lacking despite the substantial differences in crosstalk mechanisms and severity across hardware architectures.
method: The authors conducted a systematic literature review covering crosstalk in contemporary quantum devices, synthesizing theoretical frameworks from Sarovar et al. and platform-specific experimental work. They organized the review by platform, discussing characterization techniques (simultaneous randomized benchmarking, idle tomography, Rabi ratios), mitigation approaches (architectural design, tuning, compilation, dynamical decoupling), and security implications (pulse spillover attacks, always-on interaction attacks, crosstalk-enabled spying).
result: The review identifies six major classes of crosstalk mechanisms across platforms: superconducting devices show always-on $ZZ$ coupling and gate spillover; trapped ions exhibit measurement photon reabsorption and MS gate spillover; neutral atoms suffer Van der Waals interactions and readout detector blurring; photonic systems experience phase-shifter thermal crosstalk; semiconductors encounter frequency crowding and heating effects; NV centres face frequency crowding from nuclear spins spanning 220–480 kHz over non-uniform spacing. Mitigation success ranges from flux crosstalk reduction of 56.5% to 0.13% (MZLC protocol) to fidelity improvements from 0.49 to 0.99 via reinforcement learning-based qubit allocation, with open challenges remaining in coherent crosstalk treatment for quantum error correction at scale.
